prompt: Which of these does the model see when it decides whether to call get_order?

choices.text: The code of shop.get_order
choices.why: The function is never sent. The model sees only the definition.

choices.text: The tool's name, description and input schema
choices.why: Right. Those three travel with every request, and they are all the model has to go on.

choices.text: A sample of rows from shop.db, so it knows what an order looks like
choices.why: No data is sent until a call is made and its result returned.

choices.text: Nothing until it calls it
choices.why: The definitions are part of every request, before any call.

prompt: Why does tools.py read the list of genres from books.jsonl instead of typing it into the schema?

choices.text: Because JSON Schema enums cannot be written by hand
choices.why: They can; the point is keeping them true.

choices.text: To make the schema smaller
choices.why: The list is the same size either way.

choices.text: So the enum cannot drift from the catalogue
choices.why: Right. A genre added to the books is allowed at once, and a typed list would silently refuse it.

choices.text: Because the model insists on reading data files before it calls a tool
choices.why: The model reads only the definition; the file is read by the host when tools.py loads.

prompt: The description of get_order states the id's format in words, and the schema enforces it with a pattern. Why both?

choices.text: Because providers reject a pattern unless the description repeats it
choices.why: No provider requires that. The two do different jobs.

choices.text: The description prevents the mistake; the schema catches it
choices.why: Right. One helps the model get it right; the other is the host's check when it does not.

choices.text: Because the description is shown to the customer and the schema is not
choices.why: Neither is shown to the customer.

choices.text: For redundancy in case one is lost in transit
choices.why: Both travel in the same request; neither is lost.

prompt: A colleague adds 'Only call this after the customer confirms' to issue_refund's description. What is wrong with relying on it?

choices.text: Descriptions longer than one sentence are truncated by providers
choices.why: Descriptions can be several sentences long. Length is not the problem.

choices.text: The model will refuse to call the tool at all
choices.why: It may call it or not; that uncertainty is the problem.

choices.text: Customers can read tool descriptions
choices.why: They cannot. The description goes to the provider and the trace, not to the customer.

choices.text: It is a request the model may ignore; the host has to enforce it
choices.why: Right. A rule that matters lives in code the model cannot skip, which is lesson 17's design.

prompt: Match each schema keyword to the call it refuses.
get_order("M-9999") passed the schema and failed in the function. What does that show?

choices.text: A schema checks form, never facts
choices.why: Right. M-9999 has the right shape; whether it exists is the function's to say.

choices.text: That the pattern ^M-[0-9]{4}$ is wrong and should list the real ids
choices.why: A pattern listing every id would be a copy of the database inside the schema.

choices.text: That the validator was skipped for that call by mistake
choices.why: The validator ran and passed it; the function then raised LookupError.

choices.text: That shop.db is out of date
choices.why: M-9999 was never an order: make_shop.py writes M-1041 to M-1048.

prompt: Why does the lesson say a provider's strict mode does not replace the host's validation?

choices.text: Because strict mode makes requests too slow to be usable in an agent loop
choices.why: Speed is not the argument made.

choices.text: Because strict mode is available only on the most expensive models
choices.why: Availability varies; the argument holds wherever it is available.

choices.text: Because strict mode ignores the required keyword
choices.why: It honours required; its limits are elsewhere.

choices.text: It is the provider's promise over a subset of JSON Schema; the host is the last place to refuse
choices.why: Right. The host still owns the decision to run, and checks what is checkable before running.

prompt: Without the gate, what would `find_books(max_results="five")` have done?

choices.text: Returned five books, since Python converts the word to a number
choices.why: Python does not convert words to numbers.

choices.text: Crashed the host with a TypeError at the slice
choices.why: Right. stocked[:"five"] raises TypeError: a host failure instead of a correctable mistake.

choices.text: Returned every book in the genre
choices.why: A string in a slice does not mean 'all'; it raises.

choices.text: Asked the model to repeat the call
choices.why: Nothing asks the model anything without the gate; the exception propagates.

prompt: How many requests did agent.py send to answer 'Where is my order 1043?', the refused call included?
find_books returned one mystery, whether three or five were asked for. Why is that the right behaviour?

choices.text: Because the validator capped max_results at one
choices.why: The validator allows 1 to 10. Five passed, and three is the default.

choices.text: Because Ollama trimmed the result to save tokens
choices.why: Ollama never sees a tool run. The host calls find_books and sends what it returns.

choices.text: Only one is in stock
choices.why: Right. Two of the three mysteries with prices are sold out. An honest small answer is worth more than a padded one.

choices.text: Because the catalogue has only one mystery
choices.why: The shop prices three mysteries; it stocks only one of them.

prompt: run_tool catches LookupError and ValueError and lets other exceptions through. Why not catch everything?

choices.text: An outage turned into a polite result hides it behind a conversation that looks fine
choices.why: Right. Expected failures become results; a broken database or a bug must stop the run loudly.

choices.text: Because catching every exception is not allowed in Python
choices.why: Python allows `except Exception`; the choice is deliberate.

choices.text: Because other exceptions are too long to fit in a tool result
choices.why: Length is not the reason; what the model could do about them is.

choices.text: To save tokens on every error result sent back
choices.why: An error message costs a handful of tokens either way.

prompt: Which belong in an error message returned to the model? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Which argument failed and the rule it broke
choices.why: Yes. That is what the model needs to correct the call.

choices.text: What would succeed, such as the list of tools that exist
choices.why: Yes. It turns a dead end into a next step.

choices.text: The stack trace, so the model can see where the error happened
choices.why: No. A trace leaks paths and code, and the model can do nothing with line numbers.

choices.text: The SQL that failed
choices.why: No. Internal queries do not belong in a conversation that goes to a provider and into traces.

prompt: After get_order returned `LookupError: no order M-9999`, what did the model do?

choices.text: Retried with M-9998, the closest id
choices.why: It guessed no other id; it asked the customer.

choices.text: Asked the customer to check the number
choices.why: Right. It said the order does not exist and asked for something to find it by, which is what an error result makes possible.

choices.text: Crashed the run with an exception that the host printed
choices.why: run_tool turned the exception into an error result; nothing crashed.

choices.text: Said the order had been delivered
choices.why: That would be a fact nobody fetched.

prompt: A loop checks the finish reason to decide whether to run tools. Why does that loop never run tools called through Ollama's own /api/chat?

choices.text: Because Ollama's own API does not support tool calls
choices.why: It does: wires.py got a call back from /api/chat.

choices.text: Because the call arrives in a second reply the loop never reads
choices.why: The call is in the same message, in tool_calls.

choices.text: A reply with a call still ends with done_reason stop
choices.why: Right. The loop has to look for the calls themselves, as it must with Gemini's STOP.

choices.text: Because done_reason is only filled in when streaming
choices.why: wires.py did not stream, and done_reason came back as stop.

prompt: In OpenAI's Chat Completions, what type are a tool call's arguments when they arrive?

choices.text: A JSON object that is ready to use as a Python dict
choices.why: They arrive as a string, which the program has to parse.

choices.text: A string containing JSON
choices.why: Right. function.arguments is a string, and now and then a model produces one that does not parse.

choices.text: A list of positional values in the order the parameters were declared
choices.why: Arguments are named, never positional, on all three wires.

choices.text: Protocol buffer bytes
choices.why: The wire is JSON.

prompt: Match each provider to how a tool result goes back to the model.

pairs.right: A message with role tool and tool_call_id
A functionResponse part with name and id

prompt: With `--drop-one`, Anthropic's API would refuse the next request with a 400; the stand-in accepted it. What is wrong with that request?

choices.text: The two calls should have been made in separate replies
choices.why: Two calls in one reply are allowed; their results are the problem.

choices.text: The first result was too large
choices.why: Size was not the complaint. A result was missing.

choices.text: The model's reply was not appended
choices.why: It was; that is why the call with no result is in the conversation at all.

choices.text: A tool_use id had no tool_result with that id in the next message
choices.why: Right. Every call needs its result; a tool that cannot run still gets one, marked as an error.

prompt: A model asks, in one reply, for get_order(M-1043) and issue_refund on the same order. What does the lesson suggest a host do?

choices.text: Run both at once, to save time
choices.why: The refund would be decided before the lookup that justifies it has returned.

choices.text: Run the read, and hold the write for a later step, one at a time
choices.why: Right. Reads run together safely; writes run one at a time, after what justifies them.

choices.text: Refuse the whole reply and end the run
choices.why: The read is useful; ending the run throws it away.

choices.text: Run the refund first, then the lookup
choices.why: That is the most dangerous order.

prompt: How many cents were refunded in total across the three issue_refund calls in the transcript?
Why is a key the model invents on each call useless as an idempotency key?

choices.text: Because models write keys that are too short
choices.why: A long invented key has the same problem.

choices.text: Because keys must be numbers, and models tend to write words
choices.why: issue_refund accepts any string of 8 or more characters.

choices.text: A retry invents a new key, so it looks like a new intent
choices.why: Right. The key must identify the intent, and come from something that exists before the run, such as the ticket.

choices.text: Because the provider rejects keys it did not issue
choices.why: The key is the host's business; the provider never sees it as a key.
